courseTitle: Quantum Programming with Q# & Azure Quantum

lessons.title: What Q# Is & When to Reach for It

slots.practicalActivity: Write two short paragraphs answering the lesson's own 'Check yourself' scenario: a colleague prototyping a VQE that needs scipy in a tight loop with the quantum circuit, and a colleague who needs a credible physical-qubit-count estimate for a grant proposal on an algorithm that won't run for years. Name the specific toolchain feature (Qiskit's Python-native object model vs. the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator) doing the work in each case, not just the tool name.
slots.deliverable: A two-paragraph written recommendation naming the right toolchain for each of the two colleagues and the specific feature justifying each choice.

lessons.title: Setting Up the Q# Development Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Install the Azure Quantum Development Kit (QDK) VS Code extension, create the minimal project layout from the lesson (qsharp.json plus src/Main.qs), paste in the sample Main operation with @EntryPoint(), and click the Run code lens to execute it against the local simulator. Separately, pip install qsharp qsharp-widgets and run the same operation from a %%qsharp Jupyter cell to confirm both entry points compile the identical language.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or terminal transcript showing the sample operation running successfully through both the VS Code Run lens and a Jupyter %%qsharp cell.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a small Q# file with one function (pure, classical, e.g. computing a square) and one operation (allocates a qubit, applies H, measures). Then deliberately try calling H from inside the function to trigger the compiler error the lesson describes, and write down the exact rejection reason. Finally write a repeat-until loop that flips a qubit with H and retries until it measures One, tracking the attempt count exactly as the lesson's FlipUntilOne example does.
slots.deliverable: Your working .qs file with the function/operation pair and the repeat-until loop, plus a one-sentence note quoting the compiler's rejection when you tried calling an operation from a function.

slots.practicalActivity: By hand, multiply H's matrix (1/sqrt(2))*[[1,1],[1,-1]] against |0> = [1,0] to confirm the amplitude vector [0.7071..., 0.7071...], then square each amplitude to confirm P(0)=P(1)=0.5 exactly. Then run MeasureSuperposition() with qsharp.run(shots=1000) and tally the actual Zero/One counts, comparing the empirical split against your hand-computed 0.5/0.5.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-worked matrix multiplication and probability calculation, plus the actual 1000-shot tally from your run, with the two compared side by side.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement CreateBellPair() exactly as in the lab: use (q0,q1) = (Qubit(), Qubit()); H(q0); CNOT(q0,q1); measure both. Run it 1000 times via qsharp.run(shots=1000), tally all four possible (Result,Result) outcomes, and confirm empirically that (Zero,One) and (One,Zero) occur essentially never while (Zero,Zero) and (One,One) each land near 500 -- matching the lesson's exact amplitude derivation of [1/sqrt(2), 0, 0, 1/sqrt(2)].
slots.deliverable: Your CreateBellPair() source plus the real 1000-shot outcome tally, annotated with which two of the four possible pairs were expected to be impossible and whether your run confirmed that.

slots.practicalActivity: Write EntangleAll() exactly as shown (use qs = Qubit[3]; H on qs[0]; CNOT chaining through qs[1] and qs[2]), run it, then deliberately remove the final measurements so a qubit is released while still in superposition and observe the runtime error the simulator raises. Write down the exact error and explain, in your own words, why 'releasing an unresolved qubit' is treated as an error given that Qubit is opaque.
slots.deliverable: Your working EntangleAll() output plus the exact runtime error message from the deliberately-broken version, with a short explanation of why the opaque Qubit type makes that error necessary.

slots.practicalActivity: Write NormalizedAngle as a pure function (rawValue/maxValue * PI()) and EncodeValue as an operation that calls it before applying Ry. Unit-test NormalizedAngle with three plain numeric assertions (no simulator involved) to confirm the lesson's claim that function-typed classical logic can be tested with zero quantum simulation. Then answer the lesson's Check Yourself: port a Qiskit helper that both computes an angle AND appends a gate, and describe exactly what you'd have to split apart to express it legally in Q#.
slots.deliverable: Your NormalizedAngle/EncodeValue pair with the three plain-number unit-test assertions and their results, plus a written answer describing the required split for the Qiskit-helper porting scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's H|0> matrix check by hand (H's matrix times [1,0], squared amplitudes), then do the companion calculation the Check Yourself asks for: work out H|1> by hand without full matrix multiplication, reasoning only from what you know about H's effect on basis states, and state P(0)/P(1) for that case. Verify your prediction by actually running X(q); H(q); M(q) for 1000 shots.
slots.deliverable: Your hand-reasoned prediction for H|1>'s P(0)/P(1), plus the real 1000-shot tally from running X then H then M that confirms or refutes it.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement EncodeAngle(q, theta) is Adj + Ctl from the lesson (Ry(theta,q) then S(q)), then call Adjoint EncodeAngle and Controlled EncodeAngle on it as shown. Separately, try declaring an operation that calls M(q) internally as is Adj and record the compiler's rejection, then explain in writing why 'the inverse of a measurement' has no physical meaning, tying your answer to the non-unitary nature of measurement.
slots.deliverable: Your working EncodeAngle with its Adjoint/Controlled calls, plus the compiler error from the measurement-inside-is-Adj attempt and a written explanation of why it must be rejected.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full lab: PrepAngle() function returning PI()/3, PrepareState(q) is Adj+Ctl applying Ry(PrepAngle(),q), then PrepareThenUndo() calling PrepareState then Adjoint PrepareState. Hand-verify P(0)=0.75/P(1)=0.25 after PrepareState using the Ry matrix, run it 1000 times to confirm, then run PrepareThenUndo 1000 times to confirm Zero comes back with probability 1.0. Finally answer the Check Yourself: redo the math with PrepAngle returning PI()/2 instead of PI()/3.
slots.deliverable: Your three operations with their real 1000-shot results matching the hand-derived 0.75/0.25 split and the 1.0 undo-probability, plus your worked-out P(0)/P(1) for the PI()/2 variant and whether PrepareThenUndo still returns Zero with certainty.

lessons.title: Setting Up an Azure Quantum Workspace

slots.practicalActivity: Using an Azure free-tier or trial subscription, create a resource group and an Azure Quantum workspace with a linked storage account, either through the Portal flow or the az quantum workspace create CLI command shown in the lesson, adding at minimum the free resource-estimator provider. Then write out, in your own words, an answer to the lesson's Check Yourself about the teammate who thinks creating a workspace grants access to any hardware provider -- name specifically what you'd check in the workspace's provider list before trusting a real-hardware job would run.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or CLI transcript of your created workspace with its linked storage account and at least the resource-estimator provider attached, plus your written correction of the teammate's mistaken assumption.

slots.practicalActivity: List, in a table, the three target categories (simulator, resource estimator, real hardware) with one concrete reason from the lesson for using each at a specific stage of a project. Then write a short scenario (your own invented algorithm) and walk it through the realistic three-stage order the lesson describes -- simulator first, resource estimator second, real hardware only third -- explaining what would go wrong if you skipped straight to real hardware.
slots.deliverable: Your three-row target-category table plus a short written walkthrough of one invented project moving through all three stages in the correct order, naming the concrete risk of skipping ahead.

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's illustrative calculation yourself: using the simplified formula 2 x d^2 physical qubits per logical qubit, compute the total for d=15 and 6 logical qubits, confirming the lesson's 450-per-qubit and 2,700-total figures. Then redo the same formula for d=21 and 10 logical qubits (your own chosen numbers) and compare how much the physical-qubit cost grows, writing one sentence on why the quadratic scaling in d matters for a real hardware-roadmap conversation.
slots.deliverable: Your two worked calculations (reproducing the lesson's d=15/6-qubit case and your own d=21/10-qubit case) with the resulting physical-qubit totals and a sentence on what the quadratic scaling implies.

lessons.title: Submitting & Monitoring Jobs in Azure Quantum

slots.practicalActivity: Using your workspace from the earlier lesson, submit a small Q# program (e.g. your Bell-pair operation) to a simulator target via either the az quantum job submit/show/output CLI sequence or the Python Workspace.submit()/wait_until_completed()/get_results() sequence from the lesson, and capture the job moving through Waiting, Executing, and Succeeded. Then answer the lesson's Check Yourself in writing: why wait_until_completed() is fine in a script but a poor choice in an interactive notebook with a long real-hardware queue.
slots.deliverable: A transcript or screenshot of your submitted job's full lifecycle (Waiting/Executing/Succeeded) with its results, plus a written answer on the script-vs-notebook blocking tradeoff.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement MarkItem3 (Controlled Z oracle marking |11>) and a working diffusion operator, run one Grover iteration on the N=4 one-marked-item case, and confirm empirically over 1000 shots that |11> comes back with probability near 1.0 and the other three outcomes near 0 -- matching the lesson's verified [0,0,0,1.0] result. Then answer the Check Yourself: reason through what a second iteration would do to an already-fully-amplified state, without running it first, then run it to check your prediction.
slots.deliverable: Your 1000-shot tally confirming near-certain |11> after one iteration, plus your written prediction for a second iteration and the actual result you got running it, stated side by side.

lessons.title: Implementing Quantum Fourier Transform in Q#

slots.practicalActivity: Run ApplyQFT (or your own QFTByHand) on the 2-qubit input |01> and empirically confirm all four output probabilities land near 0.25 each over 1000 shots, matching the lesson's exact derivation that every amplitude has magnitude 0.5. Since measurement alone can't show you the phases (0 deg, 90 deg, 180 deg, 270 deg for k=0..3), write out by hand why QFT output is 'useless' to measure directly on its own, connecting it to why phase estimation exists as the next step.
slots.deliverable: Your 1000-shot tally showing all four outcomes near 25% each, plus a written explanation of why that flat distribution hides the phase information and what phase estimation does that direct measurement cannot.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement the full Teleport(msg, here, there) operation exactly as in the lesson, initializing msg to |+> with H, and running it with Reset calls removed from this analysis so you can verify there ends up in |+> after the classically-controlled corrections. Run it many times and confirm the four (m1,m2) outcomes each occur near 25% of the time, matching the lesson's verified result, then write a short answer to the Check Yourself on why examining there alone (without m1/m2) proves no faster-than-light signaling occurs.
slots.deliverable: Your working Teleport operation with a tally confirming the four (m1,m2) outcomes near 25% each, plus a written explanation of why the receiver's qubit alone reveals nothing without the classical bits.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement MarkItems1And3 (a single Z on the low-order qubit) and run exactly one Grover iteration on this 2-marked-item case, confirming empirically over 1000 shots that the result is close to a flat 25/25/25/25 split -- i.e. no amplification at all -- matching the lesson's verified [0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25] derivation. Then answer the Check Yourself: work out by hand or by experiment what number of iterations (if any) would actually help in this specific 2-marked-out-of-4 case, and explain why this marked-to-total ratio is unusually hard for Grover's algorithm.
slots.deliverable: Your 1000-shot tally confirming the flat/no-amplification result for one iteration, plus your worked answer on what iteration count (if any) would help and why this ratio is a hard case for Grover's algorithm.

slots.practicalActivity: Define PrepareAndMeasure() in a %%qsharp cell, call it from Python with qsharp.eval(), and print both the result and its Python type. Then run the Counter-over-a-loop pattern from the lesson for 1000 calls, compare your actual Zero/One counts against the exact 0.5/0.5 theoretical split derived from |1/sqrt(2)|^2, and write your own answer to the Check Yourself on why Qiskit never needed an equivalent bridge.
slots.deliverable: Your notebook output showing the Python type of a Q# Result value, the 1000-call Counter tally compared to the theoretical 50/50 split, and a written answer on the real cost of Q#'s separate-language design.

slots.practicalActivity: Call qsharp.init(target_profile=qsharp.TargetProfile.Base), then run qsharp.run('PrepareAndMeasure()', shots=1000) and qsharp.estimate('PrepareAndMeasure()') in the same session, printing both outputs. Then answer the Check Yourself in writing: why code that compiles under the default profile can fail under the restrictive Base profile, and why catching that locally beats discovering it after a real job submission fails.
slots.deliverable: Your session output showing both the 1000-shot run list and the resource-estimate report under the Base profile, plus a written explanation of the profile-mismatch risk and why catching it locally matters.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the exact folder layout from the lesson on disk (qsharp.json, src/Oracles.qs, src/Algorithms.qs, requirements.txt, experiments/run_grover_sweep.py) with your Grover oracle and algorithm from earlier lessons split across the two .qs files under their own namespaces. From a Python script in experiments/, call qsharp.init(project_root=...) and run one of the operations by its fully-qualified namespace path. Then deliberately edit a .qs file mid-session and verify the recompilation gotcha: confirm a stale Python reference still points at the old version until re-fetched.
slots.deliverable: Your real multi-file project directory tree plus a script output showing a successful fully-qualified-namespace call, and a short note demonstrating the stale-reference recompilation gotcha you reproduced.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement PrepareGHZ() exactly as shown (H then two CNOTs across three qubits), call it with qsharp.run(shots=1000) from Python, and tally all eight possible 3-bit outcomes with Counter. Compare your empirical counts against the lesson's independently-derived theoretical distribution (exactly 0.5 on |000> and |111>, exactly 0 on the other six), and write up what it would mean if even a handful of an 'impossible' outcome like (Zero,One,Zero) showed up on your run.
slots.deliverable: Your full 8-outcome tally from 1000 real shots compared against the theoretical 0.5/0/0/0/0/0/0/0.5 distribution, plus a written note on what a nonzero count on an 'impossible' outcome would indicate.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the same Bell-pair-preparation logic twice side by side: as a Qiskit QuantumCircuit object you can call .draw() and .depth() on, and as a Q# operation with no equivalent introspection. List three concrete things the Qiskit version lets you do that the Q# version doesn't (and vice versa), grounded in what you actually tried, not just the lesson's prose. Then write your answer to the Check Yourself: what is genuinely lost, not just gained, by Q#'s compiler-enforced model compared to Qiskit's.
slots.deliverable: Your two side-by-side implementations with a concrete three-item list of what each model lets you do that the other doesn't, plus a written answer naming what Q#'s model costs you relative to Qiskit's.

slots.practicalActivity: Count the elementary steps in your own teleportation implementation from Chapter 4 (state prep, Bell-basis change, two measurements, two corrections) and confirm you get exactly 8, matching the lesson's verified count. Then write a one-paragraph answer to the lesson's Check Yourself: what follow-up question you'd ask a team deciding between Qiskit's transpiler output and the Resource Estimator, based on the today's-hardware-vs-future-hardware distinction the lesson draws.
slots.deliverable: Your own 8-step count of the teleportation protocol's elementary operations, plus a written follow-up question you'd pose to a team conflating the two resource-estimation tools, with your reasoning.

lessons.title: Capstone: Port a Circuit Between Qiskit & Q#

slots.practicalActivity: Write both full implementations of Bell-state preparation side by side (Qiskit's QuantumCircuit(2,2) version and Q#'s PrepareAndMeasureBell() version), annotating the three translation decisions the lesson names: register declaration vs. qubit allocation, gate-call-as-method vs. direct operation call, and classical-register write vs. return-type measurement. Run both and confirm each produces the predicted 50/50 split between 00 and 11 with zero occurrences of 01/10 over 1000 shots each.
slots.deliverable: Both complete implementations with the three translation decisions annotated inline as comments, plus the two 1000-shot result tallies confirming the matching 00/11-only distribution.

lessons.title: Capstone: Wrap-Up — Choosing the Right Tool

slots.practicalActivity: Invent one realistic project scenario not already covered by the lesson's four worked examples. Using specific mechanisms you actually used in this course (the operation/function split, is Adj+Ctl functors, the Resource Estimator, circuit-as-data/transpilation) argue in writing for which tool you'd reach for and why, exactly as the lesson's four scenarios do -- not a general impression of which tool is 'better'.
slots.deliverable: A written decision-framework entry for your own invented scenario, naming the specific Q# or Qiskit mechanism that justifies the choice, in the same style as the lesson's four worked examples.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can write real Q# programs (operations, functors, resource estimation) in both the VS Code and Python/Jupyter entry points, provision and submit jobs to an Azure Quantum workspace, has reimplemented Grover's algorithm, the QFT, and teleportation in a second real toolchain, and can argue concretely -- using specific mechanisms, not vibes -- when to reach for Q#/Azure Quantum versus Qiskit on a real project.
